extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the effects, strengths, and dangers of democratic (majoritarian) government, as discussed in a comparative political-theory treatise. Focuses on participation, institutions, stability, tyranny of the majority, public opinion, and social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political activity and social agitation as a democratic advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic government produces a 'ceaseless agitation' that pervades social intercourse: meetings, societies, debates, and local public projects are common and energize the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the extent to which citizens routinely participate in public meetings, form societies (e.g., temperance societies), and engage in local improvement projects. Examples cited include church-building committees, school and road discussions, and temperance societies reducing liquor consumption (Pennsylvania example: 270,000 members; 500,000 gallon reduction). Consider both the observable bustle and the diffusion of political activity into everyday life (women attending meetings, debating clubs substituting for theatre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal participation and inclusiveness of democratic institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies the whole community, not a single class, is engaged in ameliorating social conditions; provisions are meant for 'all ranks of life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how widely participation is distributed across classes and genders, whether decision-making addresses the needs of varied social ranks, and whether institutions enable ordinary citizens (including lower orders) to exercise authority and acquire self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's indirect economic and commercial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic institutions indirectly stimulate commercial activity and private enterprise by teaching people how to promote economic activity through experience derived from legislation and public engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate correlations between civic engagement and commercial dynamism: frequency of civic deliberation, spread of ideas about private improvement, and observable increases in economic initiative attributable to democratic habits rather than specific laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutability/instability of laws inherent in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural defect of democratic institutions is the mutability of laws: frequent changes in legislature composition and broad legislative authority make laws ephemeral and alterable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for indicators such as very short legislative terms, frequent constitutional amendments, and a high volume of enacted statutes (example: Massachusetts legislative acts filling volumes). Judge the permanence of legal frameworks and whether rapid legislative turnover correlates with capricious lawmaking and administrative instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of power in the majority (absolute sovereignty of the majority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of democratic government is the absolute sovereignty of the majority; constitutions and customs may increase this power further (e.g., immediate elections, brief terms, pledged delegates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional design that magnifies majority power: direct elections, short terms of office, weak executive independence, judicial dependence on legislature (e.g., appointment/stipend control), and practices like pledged delegates which bind representatives to majority directives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom and informal practices that amplify majority control
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond law, custom (such as instructing or pledging delegates) can nullify representative safeguards and make the majority effectively deliberate in public rather than through elected intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine informal norms: whether electors impose positive obligations on delegates, whether representatives are routinely bound by constituent instructions, and how these customs affect separation of powers and representative independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral authority and presumed infallibility of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral power of the majority rests on the belief that aggregate opinion equals superior intelligence or wisdom, and the theory of equality is extended to intellect, increasing deference to majoritarian decisions over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cultural attitudes toward majority wisdom (deference to collective judgment), the social sanctioning of dissenters, and the time-based legitimization of majority rules (i.e., laws gain respect through longevity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny of the majority and lack of effective safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlimited majoritarian power can result in tyranny: majority decisions can wrong minorities, and without adequate checks a people may exceed 'the boundaries of justice and of reason.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legal and extra-legal protections for minorities: presence of independent judiciary, executive autonomy, legal recourse against unjust laws, and historical examples of majority-instigated abuses (example: Baltimore 1812 mob attacking newspaper editors; racial intimidation preventing blacks from voting despite legal rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of institutional checks (balanced legislative, executive, judicial independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy need not imply despotism if legislative, executive, and judicial powers are structured so the legislature represents the majority without being a slave to its passions, the executive retains independent authority, and the judiciary remains independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge constitutional and practical separation of powers: fixed vs. frequent turnover, appointment and tenure protections for judges, scopes of executive discretion, and whether any power has effective restraints to prevent majoritarian excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary authority of public officers under majoritarian control
rubrics_metrics.description: When the majority treats public officers as passive agents, officials may exercise arbitrary authority within ill-defined bounds and be rewarded or reprimanded at the majority's pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine clarity of office duties and remuneration, protections against popular pressure, and instances where officers exceed bounds because backed by majority opinion. Consider whether such habits threaten long-term liberty by normalizing arbitrary administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic suppression of free opinion and moral coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Majority decisions exert moral and social pressure that suppress free discussion; once the majority's decision is 'irrevocably pronounced' public discourse often ceases and dissenters are socially isolated rather than physically punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess freedom of expression in practice: social costs borne by dissenters (loss of career, esteem, political prospects), prevalence of self-censorship, and strength of social sanctions versus legal penalties. Consider whether the majority's power operates as a 'civil' despotism that enslaves minds rather than bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity vs. quality of democratic initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy tends to produce a greater number of public projects and social ameliorations with zeal and rapidity, but often with less perseverance, method, and skill than more centralized governments; it 'does a greater number of things' though not always well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both quantity and quality of public projects: look for examples where rapid majority-driven initiatives produced improvements but also neglected existing institutions (example: building new prisons while old jails deteriorated). Measure continuity, follow-through, and administrative competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of government form with societal aims (refinement vs. comfort)
rubrics_metrics.description: If society's aim is to cultivate arts, manners, and heroic virtues, democracy may be an uncertain guide; if the aim is comfort, material prosperity, and reduced crime, equalizing conditions and democracy better serve those ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or prescribing a regime, consider the prioritized social objectives (cultural refinement and high enterprises vs. material welfare and general prosperity) and whether democratic institutions are suited to those goals.
